questions.question: What does it mean for $f\colon X\to\mathbb{R}$ to be uniformly continuous?
options: For every $x\in X$, there exists an $\varepsilon \gt 0$ such that $f(x) \lt \varepsilon$.
For each $\varepsilon \gt 0$, one $\delta \gt 0$ works for every pair $x_1,x_2$ with $|x_1-x_2| \lt \delta$.
For every $\delta \gt 0$, there exists an $\varepsilon \gt 0$ such that $|x_1-x_2| \lt \delta$.
There is one fixed $\delta \gt 0$ that works for every $\varepsilon \gt 0$.

questions.question: Which phrase best captures the interpretation of uniform continuity?
options: One fixed rule for input changes works everywhere.
Different points may require unrelated local rules.
The function values must be uniformly equal.
The function must be differentiable everywhere.

questions.question: On which interval is $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$ uniformly continuous: $(0,1)$ or $(1,2)$?
options: It is uniformly continuous on $(1,2)$ but not on $(0,1)$.
It is uniformly continuous on $(0,1)$ but not on $(1,2)$.
It is uniformly continuous on both $(0,1)$ and $(1,2)$.
It is not continuous on $(1,2)$.

questions.question: Which function is uniformly continuous on its whole domain?
options: $f\colon(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=\sqrt x$
$f\colon(0,1)\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=\dfrac1x$
$f\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=x^2$
$f\colon(0,1]\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=\sin\dfrac1x$

questions.question: Which implication between uniform continuity and ordinary continuity is valid?
options: Uniform continuity implies continuity.
Continuity implies uniform continuity on every domain.
Uniform continuity implies differentiability.
Differentiability implies bounded derivative.

questions.question: What is the sequential characterisation of uniform continuity stated?
options: Every input sequence must converge to a finite limit.
Equivalent input sequences must be sent to equivalent output sequences.
Bounded input sequences must be sent to bounded output sequences.
Equivalent output sequences imply equivalent input sequences.

questions.question: Let $f$ be differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $f'$ bounded. What follows?
options: $f$ is uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.
$f$ is not uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.
$f$ must be unbounded on $(a,b)$.
$f'$ must be uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.

questions.question: A continuous function $f$ on $(a,b)$ has finite right limit $f(a^+)$ and finite left limit $f(b^-)$. What conclusion follows?
options: $f$ cannot be uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.
$f$ is uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.
$f$ must be a polynomial.
$f$ has no equivalent sequence criterion.

questions.question: Which missing assumption explains why continuity alone may not give uniform continuity?
options: The function must be written using only trigonometric functions.
A global condition like endpoint behaviour or bounded slope.
The domain must contain exactly two points.
The function must fail to be differentiable.

questions.question: Why is $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ on $(0,1)$ a boundary-type example for uniform continuity?
options: It is not a function on $(0,1)$.
It has bounded values but no derivative.
Continuous but unbounded near the missing endpoint.
It is constant near $0$.

questions.question: Suppose $(x_n)$ and $(y_n)$ are equivalent sequences in $X$ and $f$ is uniformly continuous. What should happen to $(f(x_n))$ and $(f(y_n))$?
options: They must both be constant sequences.
They must both diverge.
They cannot have the same limit.
They are also equivalent sequences.

questions.question: Which statement correctly uses the definition to show uniform continuity?
options: For each $\varepsilon \gt 0$, one $\delta \gt 0$ works for all pairs.
For each $x_1\in X$, choose a new $\delta$ after seeing $x_1$.
For each pair $x_1,x_2$, choose a new $\varepsilon$.
Check only that $f(x)$ is finite for each $x\in X$.

questions.question: What is uniform about uniform continuity?
options: A different $\delta$ is chosen at every point.
One $\delta$ works for all pairs of points in the domain.
The same $\delta$ works only near one chosen point.
Only one pair of points is checked.

questions.question: Which implication appears for uniform continuity?
options: $|x_1-x_2| \lt \delta\implies |f(x_1)-f(x_2)| \lt \varepsilon$
$|f(x_1)-f(x_2)| \lt \delta\implies |x_1-x_2| \lt \varepsilon$
$x_1=x_2\implies \delta=0$
$f(x_1)=f(x_2)$ for all pairs

questions.question: For a differentiable $f$, which claim fails?
options: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, then $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[a,b]$.
If $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[a,b]$, then it is uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.
If $f$ is uniformly continuous on $(0,1)$, then $f'$ is bounded on $(0,1)$.
If $f'$ is bounded on $(a,b)$, then $f$ is uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.

questions.question: If $f$ is uniformly continuous on $X$, what can be said about $f$ at each point of $X$?
options: $f$ is discontinuous at each point.
$f$ is unbounded at each point.
$f$ is differentiable at each point.
$f$ is continuous at each point.

questions.question: If $f'$ is bounded on $(a,b)$, what can be concluded for differentiable $f$?
options: $f$ is not continuous on $(a,b)$.
$f$ is uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.
$f$ has no finite limits.
$f$ must be unbounded.

questions.question: Which feature can make a continuous function fail to be uniformly continuous on a bounded interval?
options: Being unbounded on the bounded domain
Being constant
Having a bounded derivative
Having finite one-sided endpoint limits

questions.question: How does the sequence criterion for uniform continuity use equivalent sequences?
options: Equivalent input sequences must be sent to equivalent output sequences.
Equivalent input sequences must be sent to output sequences that diverge and whose mutual distances do not tend to zero.
Only constant input sequences are allowed.
It ignores the images of the sequences.

questions.question: Let $a<b$ be finite and let $f$ be continuous on $(a,b)$ with finite one-sided limits at both endpoints. What does its continuous extension to $[a,b]$ imply about uniform continuity of $f$ on $(a,b)$?
options: $f$ is not uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.
$f$ is not continuous on $(a,b)$.
$f$ has unbounded derivative necessarily.
$f$ is uniformly continuous on $(a,b)$.
